questions.question: How does the book define a timeseries?
questions.answer: Any data obtained via measurements at regular intervals.
questions.explanation: Stated at the start of section 13.1, with examples like daily stock prices and hourly electricity consumption.

questions.question: Which task does chapter 13 focus on?
questions.answer: Forecasting
questions.explanation: The introduction says the chapter focuses on forecasting; the other tasks are mentioned on p.376 as alternatives.

questions.question: Give one natural-phenomenon and one human-activity example of a timeseries from the page.
questions.answer: Natural: seismic activity, fish populations in a river, or the weather. Human: website visitors, a country's GDP, or credit card transactions.
questions.explanation: Both lists appear in the section 13.1 paragraph.

questions.question: What does 'temporal order is everything' imply for how you should treat timeseries data?
questions.answer: The order of samples carries the information; you cannot shuffle timesteps freely, and the future must not leak into inputs used to predict it.
questions.explanation: This is an interpretation; the book later applies it by splitting the data chronologically (p.379).

questions.question: Can you name the new kind of neural network the chapter introduces?
questions.answer: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs).
questions.explanation: Listed in 'This chapter covers'.

questions.question: Why is anomaly detection typically done with unsupervised learning?
options: Because you often don't know what kind of anomaly you're looking for, so you can't train on specific anomaly examples
Because unsupervised learning is always more accurate
Because anomalies only occur in audio streams
questions.answer: Because you often don't know what kind of anomaly you're looking for, so you can't train on specific anomaly examples
questions.explanation: This is the page's reason. Timeseries can be labeled (classification and event detection are supervised); unsupervised learning isn't 'always more accurate'; anomalies occur in any stream.

questions.question: State the chapter's forecasting problem precisely.
questions.answer: Predict the temperature 24 hours in the future, given a timeseries of hourly measurements (pressure, humidity, etc.) over the recent past from rooftop sensors.
questions.explanation: Defined at the start of section 13.2.

questions.question: Hotword detection ('Hey, Alexa') is an example of which task?
questions.answer: Event detection
questions.explanation: The page gives it as the example of event detection: identifying a specific, expected event in a continuous stream. It is not unusual (anomaly) and not a label for a whole series.

questions.question: How often were the Jena measurements recorded, how many quantities, and which years does the downloaded subset cover?
questions.answer: Every 10 minutes; 14 quantities; 2009–2016.
questions.explanation: All three facts are on the page (the original data goes back to 2003).

questions.question: What four aspects of a system's dynamics do the authors say you must understand when working with timeseries?
questions.answer: Its periodic cycles, how it trends over time, its regular regime, and its sudden spikes.
questions.explanation: Listed in the first sentence on the page.

questions.question: With one record every 10 minutes, how many raw timesteps ahead is the 24-hour target, and roughly how many records do 8 years produce?
questions.answer: 144 timesteps; about 420,000 records.
questions.explanation: 6 per hour × 24 = 144 per day; 144 × 365 × 8 ≈ 420,480, close to the 420,551 lines found on p.377 (the small difference depends on the exact start and end dates and any missing records).

questions.question: Before reading on, can you predict why a densely connected network might struggle on this problem?
questions.answer: It flattens the time window into one vector and has no built-in notion of order or recurrence, so it must learn temporal structure from scratch.
questions.explanation: The page only announces that dense and ConvNets aren't well equipped; the actual results are on p.384–387.

questions.question: How many data lines does the Jena CSV contain, and what does each line represent?
questions.answer: 420,551; each line is a timestep: a date and 14 weather-related values.
questions.explanation: Stated right after Listing 13.1.

questions.question: After discarding the 'Date Time' field, at which index is the temperature in °C?
questions.explanation: The header is Date Time, p (mbar), T (degC), …; dropping the first field puts p at index 0 and T at index 1 (matching temperature[i] = values[1] on p.378). Index 2 would be Tpot (K); 13 is wd (deg).

questions.question: Check that 420,551 records at 10-minute intervals cover about 8 years.
questions.explanation: Divide by 60 for hours (≈ 70,092) and by 24 for days (≈ 2,920.5); divide by 365.25 → ≈ 8.0 years, matching 2009–2016.

questions.question: The text says the second array holds 'the rest of the data', but raw_data (p.378) includes the temperature column too. Why is that not a problem for forecasting?
questions.answer: The target is the temperature 24 hours after the end of the input window, so using past and current temperatures as inputs does not leak the future; current temperature is in fact a strong predictor.
questions.explanation: Leakage would occur only if information from after the prediction time entered the inputs.

questions.question: What does `lines = lines[1:]` do in Listing 13.1?
options: Removes the header line so only data remains
questions.answer: Removes the header line so only data remains
questions.explanation: The header was already parsed from lines[0]; slicing from 1 keeps data rows. The Date Time column is dropped later, during parsing (split(",")[1:] on p.378).

questions.question: What shape will the temperature array created in Listing 13.2 have?
questions.explanation: np.zeros((len(lines),)) with len(lines) = 420,551.

questions.question: Can you name at least five of the 14 measured quantities and their units?
questions.answer: E.g. p (mbar), T (degC), Tpot (K), Tdew (degC), rh (%), VPmax/VPact/VPdef (mbar), sh (g/kg), H2OC (mmol/mol), rho (g/m**3), wv and max. wv (m/s), wd (deg).
questions.explanation: All are in the printed header.

questions.question: What are the shapes of raw_data and temperature after Listing 13.2 runs, and why does raw_data have len(header) - 1 columns?
questions.answer: raw_data is (420551, 14) and temperature is (420551,). The header has 15 names; the Date Time column is discarded, leaving 14.
questions.explanation: len(lines) = 420,551 (p.377); [1:] drops the date field from every line, so 14 numeric values remain per row.

questions.question: Inside the loop, which quantity does values[1] contain?
questions.answer: Temperature T (degC)
questions.explanation: values excludes the date, so values[0] is p (mbar) and values[1] is T (degC), the column the callout says is stored in temperature. The date was removed by [1:], and Tpot is values[2].

questions.question: The data is recorded every 10 minutes. How many records cover 10 days, and roughly how many cover one year?
questions.answer: 1,440 for 10 days; about 52,600 for one year.
questions.explanation: 6 per hour x 24 = 144 per day (p.378); x 10 = 1,440. Beyond the book: 144 x 365.25 is about 52,596, and eight years give about 420,768, consistent with 420,551 lines.

questions.question: What does Figure 13.1 reveal about the data, and what does it not reveal?
questions.answer: It shows a strong yearly cycle repeated over eight years and the overall range (about -20 to 35 degC). It does not show daily structure, which is hidden by the density of 420k points; that requires the 10-day zoom.
questions.explanation: The book highlights yearly periodicity here and turns to daily periodicity with Figure 13.2 on p.379.

questions.question: According to the callouts, what does raw_data contain?
questions.answer: All 14 non-date columns, including temperature
questions.explanation: The callout reads 'We store all columns (including the temperature) in the raw_data array'. The date is dropped by [1:], so it is not 15 columns, and temperature is not excluded.

questions.question: Which figure is the text calling 'Figure 10.1', and why might the number differ?
questions.answer: Figure 13.1, the full-range temperature plot. The '10.x' numbering likely comes from the previous edition, where timeseries forecasting was chapter 10.
questions.explanation: The caption on the page reads Figure 13.1; the reference in the text does not match it.

questions.question: Without running code, can you write the slice that would plot days 30 to 40 of the temperature series?
questions.answer: temperature[30*144:40*144], i.e. temperature[4320:5760].
questions.explanation: Each day is 144 timesteps, so day d starts at index 144*d.

questions.question: Why must the validation and test sets be more recent than the training set in this chapter?
options: Because the task is to predict the future from the past, and evaluation should reflect that temporal ordering
Because older data has fewer features
questions.answer: Because the task is to predict the future from the past, and evaluation should reflect that temporal ordering
questions.explanation: This is the book's stated reason. Data quality and feature count do not change over time here, and Keras has no such requirement.

questions.question: Using Listing 13.5 with len(raw_data) = 420,451, compute num_train_samples, num_val_samples and num_test_samples.
In Figure 13.2, where is daily periodicity most visible, and what tells you the period is winter?
questions.answer: In the last four days (roughly timesteps 900-1,440), where peaks and troughs repeat about every 144 steps. All temperatures are below 0 degC, down to about -22 degC.
questions.explanation: The book highlights the last four days and the cold winter month; at 144 steps per day, four days cover about 576 steps.

questions.question: Why is predicting next month's average temperature easy, while predicting the temperature 24 hours ahead is hard?
questions.answer: Averaging over a month removes short-term weather variation and leaves the reliable yearly cycle. A single value one day ahead depends on chaotic weather changes that the seasonal pattern does not capture.
questions.explanation: The book contrasts year-scale periodicity with the chaotic look of the series at the scale of days.

questions.question: According to the NOTE, which kind of cycle is especially typical of human-generated data?
questions.answer: Weekly
questions.explanation: The NOTE says daily and yearly cycles are common in general and that human-generated data also tends to feature weekly cycles. The other options are not mentioned.

questions.question: What would go wrong if you shuffled all (window, target) samples and then split them 50/25/25?
questions.answer: Validation windows would overlap heavily with training windows that start a few hours earlier or later, and their targets would sit between training targets. The model would be scored on interpolation, so validation error would be over-optimistic compared with real forecasting.
questions.explanation: Consecutive samples share most of their timesteps (p.380), and the book insists that splits reflect temporal ordering (p.379).

questions.question: Can you name, for one dataset you know (traffic, sales, energy...), its daily, weekly and yearly cycles, and say which forecasting horizon would be easiest?
questions.answer: Open-ended. For example, website traffic peaks in the evening, dips on weekends and rises before holidays; monthly totals are easier to forecast than the next hour.
questions.explanation: This applies the NOTE's advice to look for multi-timescale periodicity.

questions.question: Why are the mean and standard deviation computed only on raw_data[:num_train_samples]?
options: So that validation and test data do not influence preprocessing (no information leak)
Because the later data contains missing values
questions.answer: So that validation and test data do not influence preprocessing (no information leak)
questions.explanation: The book ties the choice to using the first 210,225 timesteps as training data. Speed, missing values and Keras requirements are not the reason.

questions.question: What is the shape of mean in Listing 13.6, and what does axis=0 mean here?
questions.answer: (14,): one mean per feature; axis=0 averages over the time axis (rows).
questions.explanation: raw_data has shape (N, 14); reducing over axis 0 leaves the feature axis.

questions.question: A training feature has mean 989 and std 8.4. What normalized value does a reading of 1,006 get? (Illustrative numbers.)
questions.explanation: Apply x' = (x - mu) / sigma from Listing 13.6.

questions.question: Why does the book generate samples on the fly instead of building an array of all windows?
questions.answer: Consecutive samples (N and N + 1) share most of their timesteps, so storing every window would duplicate the data many times. Generating them from raw_data and temperature avoids that memory cost.
questions.explanation: This is the book's stated motivation for timeseries_dataset_from_array.

questions.question: Which statement about Listing 13.6 is true?
options: It normalizes the temperature target array
It computes one mean for all features combined
It modifies raw_data in place, using per-feature training statistics
It normalizes each row (timestep) to unit norm
questions.answer: It modifies raw_data in place, using per-feature training statistics
questions.explanation: -= and /= are in place, and axis=0 gives per-feature statistics. The temperature array is untouched, and the statistics are per column, not global or per row.

questions.question: State the exact problem formulation of section 13.2.1.
questions.answer: Given data covering the previous five days, sampled once per hour, predict the temperature 24 hours later.
questions.explanation: This is quoted from the first paragraph of 13.2.1.

questions.question: Could you explain to a colleague why pressure around 1,000 and H2OC around 3 is a problem for a neural network, without using the word 'normalization'?
questions.answer: Open-ended: the large-valued input dominates weighted sums and gradient sizes, so learning is unbalanced and unstable.
questions.explanation: Self-check on the motivation given in the second paragraph.

questions.question: List the sequences generated from data = [0 1 2 3 4 5 6] with sequence_length=4.
questions.explanation: n - L + 1 = 7 - 4 + 1 = 4 windows, sliding by one step, as in the book's example with length 3.

questions.question: Compute delay for sampling_rate = 6, sequence_length = 120 and a 24-hour horizon. How many rows after the window's last input is the target?
questions.answer: delay = 6 x 143 = 858; the last input is at row offset 714, so the target is 144 rows (24 hours) after it.
questions.explanation: Last input offset = 6 x (120 - 1) = 714; 858 - 714 = 144 rows = 24 x 6.

questions.question: In the dummy example, what target is paired with the sequence starting at data[N]?
questions.answer: data[N + 3]
questions.explanation: targets=int_sequence[3:] shifts by 3, as the callout says. data[N + 2] is the last element of the window, and data[N] and data[N + 1] are inside it.

questions.question: What does sampling_rate = 6 do in the Jena datasets?
options: Starts a new window every 6 rows
Keeps one data point out of six inside each window, giving one point per hour
questions.answer: Keeps one data point out of six inside each window, giving one point per hour
questions.explanation: This is the book's definition. Window starts still advance by one row, features are not reduced, and the batch size is 256 (p.382).

questions.question: Why does the dummy example pass data=int_sequence[:-3] rather than the full int_sequence?
questions.answer: So that every generated window has a valid target. Trimming the last 3 elements of data matches the 3-element shift of targets, keeping the arrays aligned; windows that would need targets beyond 9 are never generated.
questions.explanation: The same pattern appears in Listing 13.7 as raw_data[:-delay] with temperature[delay:].

questions.question: How many batches does dummy_dataset yield, and what sizes are they?
questions.answer: Three batches, of sizes 2, 2 and 1 (five sequences in total).
questions.explanation: batch_size=2 and there are 5 windows; the last batch is partial.

questions.question: Could you write the delay for a model that uses 3 days of data sampled every 2 hours to predict the temperature 12 hours ahead, at 10-minute raw resolution?
questions.answer: r = 12 rows, L = 36 points, horizon = 6 subsampled steps: delay = 12 x (36 + 6 - 1) = 492 rows.
questions.explanation: This generalizes the book's formula delay = r x (L + h - 1), with the horizon h counted in subsampled steps.

questions.question: What start_index and end_index does each of the three datasets use?
questions.answer: Train: 0 to num_train_samples. Validation: num_train_samples to num_train_samples + num_val_samples. Test: num_train_samples + num_val_samples to the end (no end_index).
questions.explanation: These are the three bullets at the top of the page.

questions.question: What is the shape of `samples` in one full batch from train_dataset?
questions.explanation: 256 samples, each with 120 hourly timesteps of 14 features. 720 would be five days without subsampling, (256, 14) drops the time axis, and Keras puts the batch axis first.

questions.question: Why is the data argument raw_data[:-delay] rather than raw_data?
questions.answer: targets is temperature[delay:], which is delay elements shorter. Trimming the data by the same amount keeps the two arrays aligned and guarantees every window start N has a target temperature[N + delay].
questions.explanation: This is the same pattern as int_sequence[:-3] / int_sequence[3:] on p.381.

questions.question: Which statement about shuffle=True in Listing 13.7 is correct?
options: It shuffles the 120 timesteps within each window
It mixes training and validation windows
It randomizes the order of windows within each dataset's index range
questions.answer: It randomizes the order of windows within each dataset's index range
questions.explanation: Windows keep their internal order, and each dataset only draws from its own range. Shuffling timesteps or features would destroy the data's meaning.

questions.question: Approximately how many windows does train_dataset contain, and how many batches of 256 is that?
questions.answer: 210,225 - 714 = 209,511 windows, which is 819 batches (the last one partial).
questions.explanation: Each window needs 6 x 119 = 714 rows after its start, so starts run from 0 to 209,510. ceil(209,511/256) = 819. (Derived; not stated on this page.)

questions.question: In what units are the targets, and why?
questions.answer: Degrees Celsius: they come from the temperature array, which was not normalized in Listing 13.6 (only raw_data was).
questions.explanation: This is why MAE values later on (for example 2.44 on p.384) are directly in degrees.

questions.question: Could you modify Listing 13.7 to forecast 12 hours ahead from 3 days of hourly data? Which two lines change?
questions.answer: sequence_length = 72 and delay = sampling_rate * (sequence_length + 12 - 1); the dataset calls stay the same.
questions.explanation: All alignment flows from the delay formula and the window parameters.

questions.question: A dataset has 95% class A and 5% class B. What accuracy does the commonsense baseline reach?
questions.explanation: Always predicting the majority class A is correct 95% of the time, as in the book's 90/10 example. 50% would be random guessing on balanced classes, and 5% is always predicting B.

questions.question: What two properties of the temperature series justify the 'temperature in 24 h = temperature now' baseline?
questions.answer: It is continuous (tomorrow's temperatures are likely close to today's) and periodic with a daily period.
questions.explanation: These are stated directly in the second paragraph of 13.2.2.

questions.question: Compute the MAE for preds = [10, 12, 8, 15] and targets = [11, 9, 8, 13].
questions.explanation: Apply np.mean(np.abs(preds - targets)).

questions.question: Why does Listing 13.9 sum absolute errors and count samples instead of averaging per-batch MAEs?
questions.answer: Batches can differ in size (the last one is smaller). Summing all errors and dividing by the total count gives the exact mean over all samples.
questions.explanation: total_abs_err and samples_seen are initialized on this page and divided at the end on p.384.

questions.question: What does Listing 13.8 print for targets.shape?
questions.explanation: One scalar temperature per sample in the batch. (256, 1) would need an extra axis, and (256, 120) or (120,) would mean one target per timestep.

questions.question: Would the 'same as now' baseline be as good for a 12-hour horizon? Why or why not?
questions.answer: No. 12 hours later the series is at the opposite phase of the daily cycle (day vs night), so the daily swing adds to the error. The 24-hour horizon matches the daily period, which cancels that swing.
questions.explanation: This follows from the daily periodicity the book invokes to justify the baseline.

questions.question: For a problem you work on, can you name the commonsense baseline and its expected score before training anything?
questions.answer: Open-ended: for example, the majority class, the last value, the same value one period ago, or the training-set mean.
questions.explanation: Applies the book's advice that baselines are especially useful on new problems.

questions.question: In `preds = samples[:, -1, 1] * std[1] + mean[1]`, what does `samples[:, -1, 1]` select?
options: The first timestep's pressure for every sample
The last timestep's temperature (normalized) for every sample
The mean temperature over the window
questions.answer: The last timestep's temperature (normalized) for every sample
questions.explanation: Index −1 on axis 1 is the last timestep and index 1 on axis 2 is the temperature column, per the callout. It is not the first timestep, it is not the target (targets come separately), and no averaging happens.

questions.question: What validation and test MAE does the commonsense baseline achieve?
questions.answer: 2.44 °C on validation and 2.62 °C on test.
questions.explanation: Stated directly on the page; in other words, about 2.5 degrees off on average.

questions.question: Why do the authors recommend trying a small densely connected network before an RNN?
questions.answer: To make sure any extra complexity is legitimate: if a cheap model already performs as well, the expensive model's cost isn't justified, and you can attribute gains correctly.
questions.explanation: The page says this is the best way to make sure further complexity delivers real benefits, just as the commonsense baseline does for ML in general.

questions.question: Why is MSE used as the loss rather than MAE in Listing 13.10?
options: MSE is smooth around zero, which helps gradient descent
MAE cannot be computed in Keras
questions.answer: MSE is smooth around zero, which helps gradient descent
questions.explanation: That is the stated reason. MSE is in °C², not °C. Keras supports MAE (it is used as a metric). MSE actually amplifies outliers rather than ignoring them.

questions.question: Compute the number of trainable parameters of the model in Listing 13.10 given input shape (120, 14).
questions.answer: Flatten gives 1680 inputs; Dense(16): 1680·16+16 = 26,896; Dense(1): 16+1 = 17; total 26,913.
questions.explanation: A Dense layer has inputs×units weights plus units biases; Flatten has no parameters.

questions.question: Why does the last Dense layer have no activation function?
questions.answer: Because this is regression: the output must be an unrestricted real number (a temperature, possibly negative), so a linear output is used.
questions.explanation: The page notes the missing activation is typical for regression; any squashing or rectifying activation would limit the range of predictable temperatures.

questions.question: Can you explain, without looking, what save_best_only=True does in the ModelCheckpoint callback and why it matters for the later test evaluation?
questions.answer: It saves the model to jena_dense.keras only when the monitored validation loss improves, so after training the file contains the best epoch's model, which is reloaded for test evaluation.
questions.explanation: The callout says the callback saves the best-performing model; p.385 reloads it before evaluating.

questions.question: What does `model.evaluate(test_dataset)[1]` return in Listing 13.10?
questions.answer: The test MAE
questions.explanation: evaluate returns [loss, *metrics]; with metrics=['mae'], index 1 is MAE. Index 0 would be MSE, and evaluate returns neither sample counts nor epoch numbers.

questions.question: Why is the model reloaded from jena_dense.keras before evaluating on the test set?
questions.answer: Because ModelCheckpoint with save_best_only=True saved the best-performing epoch, and the in-memory model after fit() has the last epoch's weights, which overfit.
questions.explanation: The callout says 'Reloads the best model and evaluates it on the test data'; Figure 13.3 shows validation MAE rising after epoch 3.

questions.question: Looking at Figure 13.3, does the dense model beat the commonsense baseline? Justify with numbers.
questions.answer: No. Its best validation MAE is about 2.55 °C (epoch 3), above the baseline's 2.44 °C.
questions.explanation: The blue curve stays between about 2.55 and 2.73 °C; the baseline is 2.44 °C (p.384).

questions.question: What sign of overfitting does Figure 13.3 show?
options: Training MAE keeps falling while validation MAE rises after epoch 3
Validation MAE is always below training MAE
questions.answer: Training MAE keeps falling while validation MAE rises after epoch 3
questions.explanation: That divergence is the overfitting signature. Both curves don't rise. Validation is below training only at epoch 1, and the training curve is clearly falling.

questions.question: Which history keys does Listing 13.11 read, and what do they contain?
questions.answer: history.history['mae'] (per-epoch training MAE) and history.history['val_mae'] (per-epoch validation MAE).
questions.explanation: These keys exist because 'mae' was passed in metrics to compile(); the 'val_' prefix comes from validation_data in fit().

questions.question: Why is the training MAE at epoch 1 (≈ 2.9) higher than the validation MAE (≈ 2.57)?
questions.answer: Training MAE is averaged over the batches of epoch 1 while the weights are still improving from random initialization; validation MAE is measured after the epoch with the improved weights.
questions.explanation: This is a measurement-timing effect, not a sign that validation data is easier (explanation beyond the book).

questions.question: Could you rewrite Listing 13.11 to also plot the MSE loss curves on a second figure? Which keys would you use?
questions.answer: Use history.history['loss'] and history.history['val_loss'] with the same plotting calls.
questions.explanation: Self-check that you understand which history keys correspond to the loss and which to the metric.

questions.question: According to the page, why doesn't the dense model learn the commonsense solution?
options: The commonsense solution cannot be represented by a two-layer network
The solution is one of millions in the hypothesis space and gradient descent need not find it
The learning rate was too high
questions.answer: The solution is one of millions in the hypothesis space and gradient descent need not find it
questions.explanation: The page says the heuristic is 'just one model among millions' in the space (so it is representable), and existence doesn't guarantee gradient descent finds it. Learning rate and loss aren't blamed.

questions.question: What two remedies do the authors name for this limitation of machine learning?
questions.answer: Good feature engineering and relevant architecture priors.
questions.explanation: Stated at the end of the 'pretty significant limitation' paragraph: you need to tell the model precisely what to look for.

questions.question: State the translation invariance assumption for sequences and give one reason it might not hold for weather data.
questions.answer: A sliding window's content should have the same properties regardless of its location. For weather, recent data is more predictive than old data, and morning and evening patterns differ, so position matters.
questions.explanation: The definition is on this page; p.387 develops why weather violates it.

questions.question: Given input shape (120, 14), what is the output shape and parameter count of Conv1D(8, 24) with default valid padding, and what does MaxPooling1D(2) produce?
questions.answer: (97, 8) with 24·14·8 + 8 = 2,696 parameters; MaxPooling1D(2) gives (48, 8).
questions.explanation: Valid conv length = 120 − 24 + 1 = 97; pooling floors 97/2 to 48.

questions.question: Why was a window length of 24 chosen for the first Conv1D?
options: So that each window covers 24 hours, one daily cycle
To match the 24-hour prediction delay exactly
questions.answer: So that each window covers 24 hours, one daily cycle
questions.explanation: The page says 'we look at 24 hours of data at a time (one cycle)'. There are 14 features, not 24. The batch size has nothing to do with it. The delay isn't the stated reason.

questions.question: Why does Keras have no SeparableConv3D layer?
questions.answer: Not for any theoretical reason; it simply hasn't been implemented (footnote 2).
questions.explanation: Directly from the footnote.

questions.question: Can you explain in your own words the difference between 'the model can represent a solution' and 'the model will learn that solution'?
questions.answer: Representation is about the hypothesis space; learning depends on the optimizer, the initialization, the data and the priors that guide the search.
questions.explanation: Self-check on the page's central argument.

questions.question: Which layer in the convnet completely removes information about when a pattern occurred?
questions.answer: GlobalAveragePooling1D
questions.explanation: It averages each channel over all timesteps, which is permutation-invariant. MaxPooling1D(2) only coarsens resolution locally. Conv1D keeps positions. Dense(1) operates after the time axis is gone.

questions.question: What validation MAE does the text report for the convnet, and how does it compare with the dense model and the baseline?
questions.answer: About 2.9 °C, worse than the dense model (~2.55 °C best) and far from the 2.44 °C baseline.
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph after Figure 13.4; note the figure's curve actually stays around 3.05 °C or higher.

questions.question: Explain the first reason the authors give for the convnet's failure.
questions.answer: Weather data doesn't respect the translation invariance assumption: although it has daily cycles, morning data behaves differently from evening or night data, so the same pattern has different meaning at different positions.
questions.explanation: Convolutions share weights across positions, which assumes position doesn't change meaning.

questions.question: Trace the time dimension from 120 through Conv1D(24) → MaxPool(2) → Conv1D(12) → MaxPool(2) → Conv1D(6), with valid padding.
Why do kernel sizes shrink from 24 to 12 to 6?
options: To reduce overfitting by using fewer parameters
Because each MaxPooling1D halves the resolution, so smaller kernels still cover about 24 hours
Because later layers need fewer features
questions.answer: Because each MaxPooling1D halves the resolution, so smaller kernels still cover about 24 hours
questions.explanation: p.386 says the window is reduced as the sequences are downsampled. Parameter count and filter count aren't the reason (filters stay at 8), and Keras imposes no such rule.

questions.question: Figure 13.4 shows training MAE ending around 2.38, below the baseline. Why doesn't that mean the convnet beat the baseline?
questions.answer: Training MAE measures fit to data the model was trained on; the baseline comparison must use validation/test data, where the convnet is around 3.0 °C.
questions.explanation: The flat validation curve and falling training curve show that what was learned doesn't generalize.

questions.question: Before reading p.388, can you guess the second reason the convnet fails, based on the architecture?
questions.answer: Order matters: recent data is much more informative, and pooling (especially global average pooling) destroys order information.
questions.explanation: Self-check; p.388 confirms this as the second reason.

questions.question: What are the two reasons the book gives for the 1D convnet's poor performance?
questions.answer: (1) Weather data is translation invariant only at a specific timescale (morning, evening and night differ); (2) order matters, since recent data is more informative, and the pooling layers destroy order information.
questions.explanation: Both bullets span p.387–388.

questions.question: According to the page, what did the densely connected approach do wrong?
options: It flattened the timeseries, removing the notion of time
questions.answer: It flattened the timeseries, removing the notion of time
questions.explanation: Stated in section 13.3's first paragraph. Pooling was the convnet's problem; unit count and loss weren't blamed.

questions.question: By what percentage does the LSTM improve on the baseline's validation and test MAE?
questions.explanation: Uses the baseline values from p.384 and the LSTM values on this page.

questions.question: Why is a recurrent network a better architecture prior than a convnet for this task?
questions.answer: It processes the sequence in order and maintains a state, respecting causality and letting recent observations dominate, whereas the convnet treats all positions alike and pools away order.
questions.explanation: The page says to look at the data 'as what it is: a sequence, where causality and order matter'.

questions.question: What does the last line of Listing 13.12, as printed, actually output?
options: The test MAE to two decimals
questions.answer: The literal string 'Test MAE: {model.evaluate(test_dataset)[1]:.2f}'
questions.explanation: Without the f prefix Python does not interpolate the braces. It's valid syntax, so there's no error, and evaluate is never called, so neither MAE nor MSE is printed.

questions.question: How many parameters does LSTM(16) have on inputs with 14 features, and how many does the whole model have?
questions.explanation: An LSTM has four transforms, each with input kernel, recurrent kernel and bias (formula beyond the book).

questions.question: Can you summarize, in one sentence each, what the dense model, the convnet and the LSTM do with the time axis?
questions.answer: Dense: flattens it away; convnet: shares filters over it, then pools it away; LSTM: reads it step by step in order, keeping a state.
questions.explanation: Self-check on the page's comparison.

questions.question: Why is epoch 1 omitted from Figure 13.5?
questions.answer: Its training MAE was very high (7.75), which would distort the plot's scale.
questions.explanation: Stated in the figure caption.

questions.question: What does the book mean by saying dense networks and ConvNets 'have no memory'?
options: Each input is processed independently with no state kept between inputs
They forget their training after each epoch
questions.answer: Each input is processed independently with no state kept between inputs
questions.explanation: That is the book's definition. Weights are stored and persist across epochs, and ConvNets handle images well.

questions.question: How did the dense model of p.384 handle the sequence, and why does that make it a feedforward approach?
questions.answer: It flattened five days of data into one large vector and processed it in one go, so the whole sequence became a single data point processed in one pass with no state.
questions.explanation: The page uses exactly this example to illustrate feedforward networks.

questions.question: In one sentence, how does an RNN process a sequence according to the page?
questions.answer: It iterates through the sequence elements while maintaining a state containing information about what it has seen so far, an internal loop.
questions.explanation: Direct paraphrase of the RNN definition.

questions.question: Based on Figure 13.5, around which epochs does the LSTM reach its best validation MAE?
questions.answer: Epochs 4–5
questions.explanation: Validation MAE is lowest (≈ 2.40) at epochs 4–5. At epoch 2 it is still about 2.58, and by epochs 8 and 10 it has risen to about 2.43 and 2.47.

questions.question: What does the reading analogy capture about RNNs, and what does 'extremely simplified' warn against?
questions.answer: It captures incremental processing with a continually updated internal summary; 'extremely simplified' warns that an RNN is a crude mechanism, not a model of biological cognition.
questions.explanation: The page draws the analogy and then qualifies it.

questions.question: Could you sketch, with arrows, the difference between how the dense model and an RNN consume a (120, 14) window?
questions.answer: Dense: (120,14) → flatten → one pass. RNN: x_1 → step → h_1, x_2 + h_1 → step → h_2, …, h_120 → output.
questions.explanation: Self-check; compare with Figure 13.6 on p.390.

questions.question: According to the page, what happens to the RNN's state between two independent samples in a batch?
options: It is carried over so the second sample benefits from the first
It is averaged across the batch
It is stored as a learned parameter
questions.answer: It is reset
questions.explanation: The page states the state is reset between two different, independent sequences such as two samples in a batch. Carrying it over would leak information between unrelated samples; averaging is not done; and the state is an activation, not a parameter.

questions.question: Why is the initial state an all-zero vector?
questions.answer: Because at the first timestep there is no previous output to use as the state, so the network starts from zeros.
questions.explanation: The page explains that the state is the previous output, which is undefined at the first step; hence an all-zero initial state.

questions.question: With input_features = 32 (this page) and output_features = 64 (p.391), what are the shapes of W, U and b in Listing 13.14, and how many parameters do they hold in total?
questions.explanation: dot(W, input_t) must map a 32-vector to a 64-vector, so W is 64x32; dot(U, state_t) maps the 64-dimensional state to 64, so U is 64x64; b matches the output size.

questions.question: In what sense is the RNN step 'similar to the transformation operated by a densely connected layer'? What is the one difference?
questions.answer: Both compute activation(dot(weights, input) + bias). The RNN adds a second term dot(U, state_t) that feeds the previous output back in.
questions.explanation: The page parameterizes f by W, U and b and calls it similar to a Dense layer; the U-term on the state is the recurrent addition.

questions.question: In Listing 13.13, which line makes the network 'recurrent'?
questions.answer: state_t = output_t
questions.explanation: Copying the output into the state is what feeds the network's own output back as input at the next step (callout: "The previous output becomes the state for the next iteration"). The first line only initializes; the loop alone would also exist in a non-recurrent per-step model; and f without the state update would never see past outputs.

questions.question: Does using an RNN change how many training samples you get from a dataset of sequences? Explain using the page.
questions.answer: No. Each sequence is still one data point, a single input to the network; only its internal processing changes from one step to a loop over elements.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph makes this point explicitly.

questions.question: Without looking, write the four-line pseudocode of the simple RNN with W, U and b, and say the shape of each variable for the NumPy example.
questions.answer: state_t = 0; for input_t in input_sequence: output_t = activation(dot(W, input_t) + dot(U, state_t) + b); state_t = output_t. input_sequence (100, 32), input_t (32,), state_t and output_t (64,), W (64, 32), U (64, 64), b (64,).
questions.explanation: Compare with Listing 13.14 and the shapes on p.391.

questions.question: In Listing 13.15, what is the shape of U?
questions.explanation: U = np.random.random((output_features, output_features)) with output_features = 64. (64, 32) is W; (32, 64) would be the transposed W used in the row-vector step function; (100, 64) is the intended shape of the output sequence.

questions.question: Summarize, in the book's words, what an RNN is.
questions.answer: A for loop that reuses quantities computed during the previous iteration of the loop, nothing more.
questions.explanation: This is the summary sentence right after the listing.

questions.question: What characterizes different RNN variants, according to the page?
questions.answer: Their step function: the computation performed at each timestep.
questions.explanation: The page says RNNs are characterized by their step function, and gives the simple RNN's as the example.

questions.question: Scalar simple RNN with W = 1, U = 0.5, b = 0, tanh, zero initial state. Compute the outputs for inputs [1, 0].
questions.explanation: At step 1 the state term is zero; at step 2 the input is zero, so only the remembered state contributes, scaled by U and squashed.

questions.question: What does np.concatenate(successive_outputs, axis=0) return when successive_outputs holds 100 arrays of shape (64,)?
questions.answer: An array of shape (6400,)
questions.explanation: Concatenating 1-D arrays along their only axis joins them end to end. (100, 64) is what np.stack would produce and what the callout claims; (64, 100) would need a transpose; concatenate always returns an array, not a list.

questions.question: In figure 13.7, where does 'State t' come from and where does 'output t' go?
questions.answer: State t is the previous output (output t-1) arriving from the left cell; output t goes upward as the step's output and rightward as State t+1.
questions.explanation: The figure shows the output of each cell branching into the output line and the next cell's state input.

questions.question: Could you replace np.tanh with another activation in the listing? What might go wrong with relu?
questions.answer: Yes, the callout says any activation could be used. With relu, outputs are unbounded, so a state fed back through U can grow without limit over many timesteps; tanh keeps it in (-1, 1).
questions.explanation: The first half is from the callout; the relu caveat is an added explanation.

questions.question: What is the output shape of layers.SimpleRNN(16) applied to keras.Input(shape=(120, 14)) with default arguments?
questions.answer: (None, 16)
questions.explanation: return_sequences=False is the default, so only the last output (16 units) is returned with a batch axis of None. (None, 120, 16) is the return_sequences=True shape; (120, 16) omits the batch axis; 14 is the input feature count.

questions.question: How do you allow a Keras RNN model to process sequences of arbitrary length?
questions.answer: Set the timesteps entry of keras.Input's shape to None, e.g. keras.Input(shape=(None, num_features)).
questions.explanation: Listing 13.16.

questions.question: Why can the last output of an RNN be used as a summary of the entire sequence?
questions.answer: Because each output at timestep t depends on inputs 0..t through the recurrent state, so the last output depends on the whole sequence.
questions.explanation: This is the NOTE at the top of the page.

questions.question: Give two reasons from the page to specify a complete input shape when all sequences have the same length.
questions.answer: model.summary() can display output length information, and it can unlock performance optimizations.
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph after Listing 13.16, with a pointer to the runtime-performance sidebar.

questions.question: Which recurrent layers support return_sequences, according to the page?
options: None; it is a model-level option
questions.answer: SimpleRNN, LSTM and GRU
questions.explanation: The page says all recurrent layers in Keras (SimpleRNN, LSTM, GRU) can run in the two modes, controlled by the return_sequences constructor argument. It is a layer argument, not a model option.

questions.question: How many trainable parameters does SimpleRNN(16) have on inputs with 14 features?
questions.explanation: Kernel W (14 x 16), recurrent kernel U (16 x 16), bias (16), following the W, U, b parameterization of p.390. The count is independent of the 120 timesteps.

questions.question: Can you say, for a model consisting of two stacked SimpleRNN layers and a Dense(1) head, which return_sequences value each RNN needs?
questions.answer: The first RNN needs return_sequences=True (the next RNN needs a sequence); the second can use the default False so Dense(1) receives a rank-2 tensor.
questions.explanation: Follows from the two modes on this page; the stacking listing is on p.393.

questions.question: In Listing 13.19, which layers need return_sequences=True?
questions.answer: The first two
questions.explanation: Intermediate layers must return full sequences so the next recurrent layer has a sequence to iterate over. The last layer can return only its last output, so 'all three' is unnecessary; 'only the first' would break the third layer; 'only the last' would break both later layers.

questions.question: What output shape does Listing 13.18 print, and why?
questions.answer: (None, 120, 16): with return_sequences=True, the layer returns a 16-unit output for each of the 120 timesteps, with an unspecified batch size.
questions.explanation: Directly shown in the listing.

questions.question: Why can't SimpleRNN learn long-term dependencies in practice, even though it can represent them in theory?
questions.answer: Because of the vanishing gradients problem: the training signal for relationships spanning many timesteps shrinks as it is propagated back through many steps, as in a very deep feedforward network.
questions.explanation: This is the page's explanation; the multiplication-of-factors detail is added in the notes.

questions.question: What does the conveyor-belt analogy describe?
options: The LSTM's way of carrying information across many timesteps
questions.answer: The LSTM's way of carrying information across many timesteps
questions.explanation: Information jumps on the belt, travels to a later timestep and jumps off intact. It has nothing to do with the batch axis, stacking, or dropout.

questions.question: Who developed the LSTM algorithm and when, according to the page?
questions.answer: Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber, in 1997.
questions.explanation: Stated in the text with footnote 4 (Neural Computation 9, no. 8, 1997).

questions.question: What feedforward-network phenomenon does the page compare the RNN vanishing-gradient problem to, and what later architectural idea is the LSTM compared to on the next page?
questions.answer: Very deep feedforward networks becoming untrainable as layers are added; the LSTM's carry is compared to residual connections.
questions.explanation: The comparison to deep networks is on this page; the sentence 'This should remind you of residual connections' finishes on p.394.

questions.question: Can you write a stacked model with two LSTM layers of 32 units on (120, 14) inputs followed by Dense(1), setting return_sequences correctly?
questions.answer: inputs = keras.Input(shape=(120, 14)); x = layers.LSTM(32, return_sequences=True)(inputs); x = layers.LSTM(32)(x); outputs = layers.Dense(1)(x).
questions.explanation: Same pattern as Listing 13.19 with LSTM, which shares SimpleRNN's API.

questions.question: What does the subscript o in Wo and Uo stand for?
questions.answer: Output
questions.explanation: The authors index the SimpleRNN cell's matrices with o for output, because more weight matrices will be added. The others are not used by the book.

questions.question: Write the output equation of the cell in figure 13.9.
questions.answer: output_t = activation(Wo · input_t + Uo · state_t + Vo · c_t + bo).
questions.explanation: Read from the middle cell of figure 13.9.

questions.question: Name the two ways in which the carry affects the cell, according to the page.
questions.answer: It is combined with the input and recurrent connections via a dense transformation, and it affects the state sent to the next timestep via an activation function and a multiplication.
questions.explanation: Stated directly in the paragraph introducing C_t.

questions.question: Why do the authors say the LSTM carry is 'pretty much the same idea' as residual connections?
questions.answer: Both give information a separate path that bypasses repeated transformations, so it (and the gradient) is not progressively degraded: residual connections across layers, the carry across timesteps.
questions.explanation: The book states the analogy; the gradient-flow explanation is added in the notes.

questions.question: Which statement about figure 13.9 is correct?
options: Each cell receives both State t and c t
The carry only flows backward in time
Figure 13.9 shows how the next carry is computed
questions.answer: Each cell receives both State t and c t
questions.explanation: Both arrows enter the middle cell. The carry does not replace the state, it flows forward along the top track, and its update rule is deferred to p.395.

questions.question: Scalar cell: Wo = 0.5, Uo = 0.5, Vo = 1, bo = 0, activation tanh, input_t = 0, state_t = 0, c_t = 2. Compute output_t with and without the carry term.
questions.answer: Without: tanh(0) = 0. With: tanh(2) ≈ 0.964.
questions.explanation: The carry contributes Vo · c_t = 2 inside the activation, showing how stored information resurfaces.

questions.question: Can you sketch figure 13.9 from memory and label State t, c t, input t and output t?
questions.answer: Three cells in a row; inputs from below, outputs above; state arrows between neighbouring cells; a carry track along the top feeding c t into each cell.
questions.explanation: Compare your sketch with figure 13.9.

questions.question: How is the next carry computed in Listing 13.21?
questions.answer: c_t+1 = i_t * k_t + c_t * f_t
questions.explanation: The book combines the three transformations with the current carry. The plain sum ignores c_t; the activation form is the output's carry term, not the carry update; and output_t is the next state, not the carry.

questions.question: What form do the three carry-update transformations have?
questions.answer: The form of a SimpleRNN cell: y = activation(dot(state_t, U) + dot(input_t, W) + b), each with its own weights.
questions.explanation: Stated at the top of the page.

questions.question: With c_t = 2, f_t = 0.5, i_t = 0.5, k_t = 0.7, compute the next carry. What values of f_t and i_t would keep the carry exactly at 2?
questions.explanation: Apply c_t+1 = i_t * k_t + c_t * f_t elementwise.

questions.question: Why does the additive form of the carry update help information survive many timesteps?
questions.answer: Because the old carry is passed on scaled only by f_t and added to new content, rather than being squashed through a nonlinearity and multiplied by a recurrent matrix at every step; with f_t near 1 it passes through nearly intact.
questions.explanation: Connects Listing 13.21 to the conveyor belt (p.393) and vanishing gradients; the gradient argument is an added explanation.

questions.question: How many distinct weight sets (each with its own W, U and b) appear in Listing 13.20?
questions.answer: Four
questions.explanation: o, i, f and k. 'Three' counts only the carry-update transformations and forgets the output transformation; one or two would mean shared weights, which the book rules out.

questions.question: What does figure 13.10 add compared with figure 13.9?
questions.answer: A 'Compute new carry' block between consecutive cells, which takes c t and the cell's inputs and produces c t+1 on the carry track.
questions.explanation: Compare the two figures on pp.394-395.

questions.question: Can you write all five LSTM equations of Listings 13.20-13.21 from memory and say which ones read the carry?
questions.answer: output_t, i_t, f_t, k_t as in Listing 13.20 and c_t+1 = i_t * k_t + c_t * f_t. output_t reads C_t through Vo; the carry update reads c_t directly.
questions.explanation: Check against the listings.

questions.question: According to the authors, what does the specification of an RNN cell (its combination of operations) determine?
options: Exactly what each gate does after training
The hypothesis space searched during training, i.e. constraints on the search
The optimal learning rate for the layer
Nothing at all; architecture is irrelevant
questions.answer: The hypothesis space searched during training, i.e. constraints on the search
questions.explanation: The page says the specification 'determines your hypothesis space ... but it doesn't determine what the cell does; that is up to the cell weights.' It is not irrelevant (it constrains the search), it does not fix gate behavior, and it says nothing about learning rates.

questions.question: What single purpose of the LSTM cell do the authors ask you to keep in mind?
questions.answer: To allow past information to be reinjected at a later time, thus fighting the vanishing gradients problem.
questions.explanation: This is the closing sentence of the second paragraph; it replaces the need to understand the cell's internal architecture.

questions.question: Why do the authors say interpretations such as 'c_t * f_t forgets irrelevant information' don't mean much?
questions.answer: Because what the operations actually do is determined by the learned weights, which are trained end to end and start over each training round, so no operation can be credited with a specific purpose; the same cell with different weights can do very different things.
questions.explanation: The equations only constrain the space of functions; gradient descent assigns roles implicitly through the weights, and nothing forces it to match human labels.

questions.question: Which pairing of technique and stated benefit/cost matches the page?
options: Recurrent dropout: increases representational power at higher compute
Stacking recurrent layers: increases representational power at the cost of higher computational loads
Bidirectional layers: fights overfitting by zeroing units
Stacking recurrent layers: mitigates forgetting by reversing the sequence
questions.answer: Stacking recurrent layers: increases representational power at the cost of higher computational loads
questions.explanation: The page lists recurrent dropout for overfitting, stacking for representational power at a compute cost, and bidirectional layers for accuracy and mitigating forgetting by presenting information in different ways. The other options swap these descriptions.

questions.question: Using c_{t+1} = i_t * k_t + c_t * f_t (elementwise), compute c_{t+1} for scalar values c_t = 2.0, f_t = 0.5, i_t = 0.4, k_t = -1.0.
questions.explanation: The old carry is halved by f_t (2.0 to 1.0) and the new term i_t * k_t = -0.4 is added. The equation is from Listing 13.21 on p.395.

questions.question: Why is it sensible to apply recurrent dropout before trying stacked recurrent layers?
questions.answer: The LSTM model overfits quickly; regularization should first bring overfitting under control. Only once the model no longer overfits and hits a performance bottleneck does adding capacity (stacking) make sense, as p.399 states.
questions.explanation: Adding capacity to a model that already overfits would make overfitting worse. The order in the page's list follows the universal workflow's advice to increase capacity until overfitting becomes the main obstacle.

questions.question: Can you explain, without looking, what the carry track is, write its update equation, and say why it helps with long sequences?
questions.answer: The carry is an additional state passed across timesteps; c_{t+1} = i_t * k_t + c_t * f_t; its additive, elementwise-scaled path lets information and gradients survive many steps, fighting vanishing gradients.
questions.explanation: If you could not, revisit p.394-395 for the construction and this page for its purpose.

questions.question: According to the page, what is the proper way to use dropout in a recurrent network?
options: Insert a Dropout layer before the recurrent layer
Sample a new dropout mask at every timestep
Apply the same dropout mask at every timestep, including a constant mask on the recurrent activations
Apply dropout only at inference time
questions.answer: Apply the same dropout mask at every timestep, including a constant mask on the recurrent activations
questions.explanation: This is Gal's prescription. Dropout before the recurrent layer hinders learning; a per-timestep mask disrupts the error signal; dropout is a training-time technique.

questions.question: What is the difference between the dropout and recurrent_dropout arguments of a Keras recurrent layer?
questions.answer: dropout is the dropout rate for the layer's input units; recurrent_dropout is the dropout rate for its recurrent units.
questions.explanation: Both are stated on the page; together they implement the two time-constant masks of Gal's method.

questions.question: Why does a temporally random dropout mask harm learning in an RNN?
questions.answer: Because it disrupts the error signal that the network propagates through time; a constant mask lets the network properly propagate its learning error across timesteps.
questions.explanation: With a changing mask, information held in a unit can be erased at any step and the gradient is computed through a different sub-network at each step. With a constant mask the network is a consistent thinned RNN.

questions.question: Compared with the first LSTM model (Listing 13.12), what two other changes accompany recurrent dropout in Listing 13.22?
options: Half the units and twice the epochs
Twice the units and five times the epochs
The same units and ten times the epochs
A GRU instead of an LSTM and the same epochs
questions.answer: Twice the units and five times the epochs
questions.explanation: LSTM(16) becomes LSTM(32) because dropout now provides regularization, and 10 epochs become 50 because dropout-regularized networks take much longer to converge.

questions.question: The LSTM in Listing 13.22 has 32 units and receives 14 input features. Using the LSTM structure of four transformations, each with W (input x units), U (units x units) and b (units), how many trainable parameters does the LSTM layer have?
questions.explanation: The four transformations (output, i, f, k on p.395) each have their own input matrix, recurrent matrix and bias. (The book's pseudocode also has a Vo term for the carry in the output; Keras's standard LSTM does not include it, which gives 6016.)

questions.question: Why can the authors afford to double the LSTM's units once dropout is added, when the 16-unit model was already overfitting?
questions.answer: Dropout provides explicit regularization, so they no longer need to rely on small network size to limit overfitting; a larger network is more expressive. Without dropout, the 32-unit network would overfit right away.
questions.explanation: The page states this reasoning in its last paragraph: 'we won't need to rely as much on network size for regularization'.

questions.question: Could you sketch, for 4 timesteps and 6 recurrent units, what a recurrent dropout mask looks like, and contrast it with the harmful alternative?
questions.answer: Correct: the same columns are zeroed in every row (timestep). Harmful: different random columns are zeroed in each row.
questions.explanation: Compare with the diagram in the visualizations section.

questions.question: The baseline test MAE is 2.62 and the dropout-regularized LSTM's test MAE is 2.45. Verify the page's 6.5% improvement figure.
questions.explanation: Relative improvement is measured against the baseline. The same computation on validation gives (2.44 - 2.27) / 2.44, about 7%.

questions.question: Why do small RNNs like those in this chapter tend to run faster on a multicore CPU than on a GPU?
options: GPUs cannot run LSTM layers at all
They involve only small matrix multiplications, and the for loop over timesteps prevents good parallelization
CPUs have more memory bandwidth than GPUs
cuDNN is only available on CPUs
questions.answer: They involve only small matrix multiplications, and the for loop over timesteps prevents good parallelization
questions.explanation: This is the sidebar's explanation. GPUs do run LSTMs (and use cuDNN for them); cuDNN is a GPU library; memory bandwidth is not the reason given.

questions.question: In Figure 13.11 the training MAE stays above the validation MAE for all 50 epochs. Why is this not a sign of a problem?
questions.answer: Training MAE is computed with dropout (recurrent and output) active, so it measures a deliberately handicapped network; validation runs without dropout. Overfitting would show as the validation curve rising, which it does not.
questions.explanation: This reasoning goes beyond the text but follows from how dropout works (p.191, p.397).

questions.question: What is a cuDNN kernel, and why do the authors call it a 'mixed blessing'?
questions.answer: A highly optimized, low-level, NVIDIA-provided implementation of the underlying algorithm (used by Keras LSTM/GRU on GPU with default arguments). It is fast but inflexible: anything it does not support causes a dramatic slowdown.
questions.explanation: Both parts are stated in the sidebar; p.399 gives recurrent dropout as an unsupported feature.

questions.question: What does the training run in Listing 13.22 use as its training loss and its monitored metric?
questions.answer: Loss MSE, metric MAE
questions.explanation: model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="mse", metrics=["mae"]). MSE is smooth around zero, which helps gradient descent (p.387); MAE is reported in degrees. This is also why the figure, which plots MAE, is mislabeled 'loss' in its caption.

questions.question: The model of Listing 13.22 uses recurrent_dropout=0.25. Based on this page and the next, what happens if you train it on a GPU?
questions.answer: Recurrent dropout is not supported by the cuDNN LSTM kernel, so Keras falls back to the regular implementation, which is generally two to five times slower on GPU, even though its computational cost is the same. For a model this small, a CPU may be faster anyway.
questions.explanation: This page says unsupported options cause a dramatic slowdown; p.399 names recurrent dropout and gives the 2-5x figure.

questions.question: Can you list, from memory, the validation and test MAE of the baseline, the first LSTM, and the dropout-regularized LSTM?
questions.answer: Baseline 2.44 / 2.62; LSTM(16) 2.39 / 2.55; dropout-regularized LSTM(32) 2.27 / 2.45.
questions.explanation: These numbers (pp.384, 388, 398) are the yardstick for the stacked and bidirectional models that follow.

questions.question: Why does adding recurrent_dropout to a Keras LSTM make it slower on GPU?
options: It doubles the number of parameters
It is not supported by the cuDNN kernel, so the layer falls back to a regular implementation that is generally 2-5x slower
It forces the model to run on CPU
questions.answer: It is not supported by the cuDNN kernel, so the layer falls back to a regular implementation that is generally 2-5x slower
questions.explanation: The page states this directly and notes that the computational cost is the same. Parameter count is unchanged, the model still runs on GPU, and unrolling is optional.

questions.question: Give the two conditions under which unrolling an RNN is viable, according to the sidebar.
questions.answer: The sequences must be relatively small (around 100 steps or fewer), because unrolling considerably increases memory consumption; and the number of timesteps must be known in advance (the Input() shape has no None entries).
questions.explanation: Both are stated in the second sidebar paragraph; the code callout repeats the second ('sequence_length cannot be None').

questions.question: The dropout-regularized LSTM no longer overfits and its validation MAE has plateaued. What does the universal workflow recommend, and why?
questions.answer: Increase capacity (more units or more layers, e.g. stacking recurrent layers), because if you aren't overfitting too badly you're likely under capacity; keep increasing until overfitting becomes the primary obstacle.
questions.explanation: This is the reasoning of the first paragraph of 13.3.5.

questions.question: A first GRU layer receives input of shape (batch, 120, 14) and is followed by a second GRU layer. What must the first layer output?
questions.answer: (batch, 120, 32), using return_sequences=True
questions.explanation: Intermediate layers must return their full output sequence, a rank-3 tensor, so the next recurrent layer has a sequence to process. A rank-2 output would give it nothing to iterate over; the other options are not valid layer outputs.

questions.question: Why does unrolling require that the number of timesteps be known in advance?
questions.answer: Because unrolling builds the computation as N explicit copies of the cell; N must be fixed when the graph is constructed, so the time axis of the Input shape cannot be None.
questions.explanation: Unrolling is 'removing the loop and simply in-lining its content N times'; a variable N cannot be in-lined.

questions.question: How does the page describe the GRU relative to the LSTM, and who introduced it?
questions.answer: As very similar to an LSTM, a slightly simpler, streamlined version of the LSTM architecture, introduced in 2014 by Cho et al.
questions.explanation: Stated in the last paragraph and footnote 6.

questions.question: Could you explain to someone why a 120-step LSTM with recurrent dropout might train faster on a CPU than on a GPU, and what you could try to speed it up on the GPU?
questions.answer: Small matrix products and a sequential loop leave the GPU underused, and recurrent dropout rules out cuDNN (2-5x slower fallback). Options: run on CPU, drop recurrent dropout to regain cuDNN, or try unroll=True (memory permitting, since 120 steps is above the suggested ~100).
questions.explanation: Combines the two halves of the sidebar (pp.398-399).

questions.question: In Listing 13.23, why does only the first GRU layer specify return_sequences=True?
options: Because the second GRU needs a full sequence as input, while the Dense head needs only the last output
To make the model use the cuDNN kernel
Because GRU layers return sequences by default
questions.answer: Because the second GRU needs a full sequence as input, while the Dense head needs only the last output
questions.explanation: Intermediate recurrent layers must output rank-3 sequences (p.399). The default is return_sequences=False; the argument is unrelated to dropout or cuDNN.

questions.question: Verify the 8.8% improvement: baseline test MAE 2.62, stacked GRU test MAE 2.39.
questions.explanation: Relative improvement over the commonsense baseline of p.384.

questions.question: Looking at Figure 13.12, at roughly which epochs is the validation MAE lowest, and what happens afterward? Why does the reported test MAE still reflect the good epochs?
questions.answer: Lowest around epochs 10-16 (about 2.25); after about epoch 20 it rises steadily to about 2.43 by epoch 50 while training MAE keeps falling, which is overfitting. ModelCheckpoint(save_best_only=True) saved the best epoch, and the listing reloads it with load_model before evaluating on the test set.
questions.explanation: The text does not mention the overfitting; it is visible in the figure. The final two lines of the listing ensure the evaluation uses the best checkpoint.

questions.question: What do the authors mean by 'diminishing returns from increasing network capacity'?
questions.answer: That adding capacity (here a second recurrent layer) now yields only a small improvement (test MAE 2.45 to 2.39), much smaller than earlier gains, so further capacity increases are unlikely to pay off much.
questions.explanation: The added layer 'does improve the results a bit, though not dramatically'.

questions.question: Which of the following did NOT change between Listing 13.22 and Listing 13.23?
questions.answer: The number of training epochs
questions.explanation: Both train for 50 epochs. The layer type (LSTM to GRU), depth (one to two) and recurrent dropout (0.25 to 0.5) all changed.

questions.question: Using the Keras GRU parameter formula 3(du + u^2 + 2u), how many parameters does the second GRU layer (32 inputs, 32 units) have?
questions.explanation: Three weight sets (update gate, reset gate, candidate), each with an input matrix, a recurrent matrix and, with reset_after=True, two bias vectors. The formula is standard Keras behavior, not stated in the book.

questions.question: Given Figure 13.12, what would you try next if you wanted a better model? Justify it with the workflow rule from p.399.
questions.answer: The model now overfits after about 20 epochs and capacity increases give diminishing returns, so stop adding capacity. Try stronger regularization, early stopping, or a different way of presenting the data, such as the bidirectional RNNs of p.401.
questions.explanation: The workflow increases capacity until overfitting becomes the primary obstacle; Figure 13.12 suggests that point has been reached.

questions.question: What happens when the first-experiment LSTM is trained on time-reversed Jena sequences?
options: It slightly beats the chronological LSTM
It strongly underperforms even the commonsense baseline
It fails to train at all
questions.answer: It strongly underperforms even the commonsense baseline
questions.explanation: This is the page's stated outcome; it shows chronological processing is important for this task. It trains, but poorly; it neither matches nor beats the forward LSTM.

questions.question: Give the two reasons the page offers for why the chronological LSTM is 'bound to outperform' the reversed one on weather data.
questions.answer: (1) The LSTM layer is typically better at remembering the recent past than the distant past; (2) the more recent weather data points are more predictive than older ones, which is also what makes the commonsense baseline strong. Read in reverse, the most predictive data is the furthest from the output.
questions.explanation: Both facts are stated on the page; together they mean the reversed model must remember the most important data across the longest distance.

questions.question: What does samples[:, ::-1, :] do to a batch of shape (batch, timesteps, features)?
questions.answer: It reverses the order of the timesteps (axis 1) in every sequence, leaving the batch and feature axes, and the targets, unchanged.
questions.explanation: ::-1 is a reversed slice applied only to the middle (time) axis.

questions.question: According to the page, why is reversed-order processing fine for natural language?
options: Because word order doesn't matter in language
Because a word's importance in understanding a sentence isn't strongly dependent on its position, so which order you use isn't crucial
Because text sequences are always short
Because LSTMs remember the distant past better on text
questions.answer: Because a word's importance in understanding a sentence isn't strongly dependent on its position, so which order you use isn't crucial
questions.explanation: The page explicitly says word order does matter; what doesn't matter is the direction. Sequence length and memory claims are not the reasons given.

questions.question: If a reversed RNN on text performs about as well as a forward one, why would combining them help at all?
questions.answer: Because they learn different representations; different yet useful representations capture aspects missed by the other, so merging them can boost performance (the ensembling intuition, p.402).
questions.explanation: Equal accuracy does not mean identical features or identical errors.

questions.question: Based on this page alone, would you expect a bidirectional LSTM to beat the plain LSTM on the Jena task? Why or why not?
questions.answer: No: the antichronological half is severely underperforming on this task (worse than the baseline), so nearly all predictive power must come from the chronological half, while the extra half adds capacity. p.402 confirms it doesn't perform as well and overfits earlier.
questions.explanation: This prediction follows from the reversed-order experiment and is confirmed by Listing 13.24's results.

questions.question: Can you think of a sequence task of your own where reading order is crucial and one where it is not? Which would benefit from a bidirectional RNN?
questions.answer: Example: forecasting tomorrow's stock volume from the last 30 days (order and direction matter; bidirectional unlikely to help) vs. classifying the sentiment of a review (direction not crucial; bidirectional likely to help).
questions.explanation: The test is whether the useful information is concentrated at one end of the sequence (direction matters) or spread throughout (direction doesn't).

questions.question: What does `layers.Bidirectional(layers.LSTM(16))` do with the LSTM instance it receives?
options: It runs that single LSTM twice, sharing weights, once forward and once backward
It creates a second, separate LSTM instance and runs one chronologically and the other on the reversed sequence
It doubles the number of units to 32 in a single forward LSTM
It reverses the input sequence and runs only one LSTM on it
questions.answer: It creates a second, separate LSTM instance and runs one chronologically and the other on the reversed sequence
questions.explanation: The page states that `Bidirectional` creates a second, separate instance of the recurrent layer. Weights are not shared (option 1). It is not one wider forward LSTM, although the concatenated output does have 32 values (option 3). It runs both directions, not just the reversed one (option 4).

questions.question: Give the two reasons the authors offer for why the bidirectional LSTM performs worse than the plain LSTM on temperature forecasting.
questions.answer: (1) All the predictive power has to come from the chronological half, because the antichronological half performs very badly on this task (the recent past matters more than the distant past). (2) The antichronological half doubles the network's capacity, so it starts overfitting much earlier.
questions.explanation: Both reasons are in the paragraph after Listing 13.24. The first relies on the p.401 experiment showing reversed processing underperforms the baseline.

questions.question: Why are bidirectional RNNs a good fit for text but not for the Jena timeseries?
questions.answer: In text, order matters but reading direction doesn't: backward reading gives an equally useful, different view, and words often depend on later context. In the weather series, the most recent readings are by far the most predictive, so the backward reader, whose memory favours the oldest steps, adds little useful information.
questions.explanation: The page says bidirectional RNNs fit data where order matters but which order you use doesn't. Combined with p.401's point that LSTMs remember the recent past better, this explains the difference.

questions.question: An `LSTM(u)` on `d` input features has $4(u(d+u)+u)$ parameters. With $u=16$ and $d=14$, how many parameters does `Bidirectional(LSTM(16))` have, and what is the output size with the default concatenation?
questions.answer: Each direction: $4(16\cdot30+16)=1{,}984$. Bidirectional: $3{,}968$ parameters. Output size: $16+16=32$.
questions.explanation: The two instances are separate, so their parameters add. Concatenating two 16-dimensional outputs gives 32. This quantifies the page's claim that the second half doubles capacity. (The formula is standard LSTM bookkeeping, not printed on the page.)

questions.question: Which concept do the authors name as the intuition behind combining chronological and reversed representations?
questions.answer: Ensembling
questions.explanation: The page says different-yet-useful representations offer a new angle on the data, which is the intuition behind ensembling (chapter 18). Regularization limits capacity, which is the opposite effect. Transfer learning reuses pretrained models. Data augmentation creates modified training samples. None of these is the stated motivation.

questions.question: Could you use a bidirectional LSTM to generate text one token at a time? Why or why not?
questions.answer: Not directly. The backward half needs the whole sequence, including future tokens, which don't exist yet during generation. Generation needs unidirectional (causal) models.
questions.explanation: This follows from how the layer works (it reads the full sequence in reverse) and is stated in chapter 14 (p.431). It explains why bidirectionality is used for classification rather than generation.

questions.question: Before adding a bidirectional layer to a new sequence problem, what quick experiment could tell you whether it's likely to help?
questions.answer: Train the same unidirectional model on reversed sequences, as on p.401. If reversed-order performance is close to chronological performance, both directions carry useful signal and bidirectionality may help. If it's much worse, the reverse half will mostly add capacity and overfitting.
questions.explanation: This is the diagnostic the book itself runs before Listing 13.24, and its outcome predicted the negative result on this page.

questions.question: According to the authors, why is about a 10% improvement over the baseline likely the best achievable on the Jena dataset?
options: The data comes from a single location, while local weather depends on patterns in surrounding locations
The dataset is too small to train an LSTM
MAE is a poor metric for temperature
questions.answer: The data comes from a single location, while local weather depends on patterns in surrounding locations
questions.explanation: The page explains that near-future weather is very predictable from a wide grid of locations but not from one station. The other options aren't claimed: RNNs handle order well, dataset size isn't mentioned as the limit, and MAE is the chapter's chosen, reasonable metric.

questions.question: Name the four kinds of changes the authors suggest trying next.
questions.answer: (1) Units per recurrent layer and dropout amount in the stacked setup; (2) Adam's learning rate or a different optimizer; (3) a stack of Dense layers as the regressor; (4) better inputs: longer or shorter sequences, a different sampling rate, or feature engineering.
questions.explanation: These are the four bullets of section 13.4.
